Interviewer asked me "How can we conduct contract testing using Playwright?" 

First correction I had to do: We cannot conduct contract testing as it natively cannot hold "consumer" & "provider" contracts. But we can explore "json-schema" validations. Which is the next best!

To understand json-schema validation we need 4 steps: 
1) Access to API spec (API Contract)
2) Create Json Schema (generate json schema using: )
3) Store json schema in your framework 
4) Use AJV/ZOD to compile schema and validate with response/request body used/received after execution of API test.

Always remember: JSON Schema validation is one technique used inside contract testing. It is not a synonym for contract testing itself.

What it covers: field presence, data types, required versus optional fields, string formats, nested structure. All of this is expressed once, declaratively, in a schema file.

What it cannot do: 

1) It cannot verify the HTTP status code or response headers were correct.
 
2) It cannot check semantic or business rules a type system cannot express, for example that end_date comes after start_date, or that a total matches the sum of line items.
 
3) It cannot tell you whether the schema reflects a real, agreed contract, or just whatever the API happened to return the one time it was sampled.

Quick tip: If you review the API spec carefully after every change made by Backend teams. Then we can use: "toJsonSchema" to dynamically generate schema using a flag. 
If set to true, it updates the schema files and we just validate the final playwright report.

KOC contracts in 2026: 6 must-have clauses
Full article in the first comment.

From January 1, 2026, Vietnam's amended Advertising Law (Law 75/2025/QH15) adds Article 15a: whoever delivers an ad to the audience also shares responsibility when that ad breaks the rules. KOC (key opinion consumer) contracts need to be tighter as a result.

Six clauses worth including:
1. Advertiser details, so the KOC can verify who is hiring them.
2. Product documents: the product notification, the label and a list of approved claims.
3. A trial period before filming. The law does not allow promoting products the KOC has not used or does not fully understand.
4. Disclosure that the content is an ad, before and during the video, with the Paid partnership label turned on.
5. A list of claims that are off limits, such as absolute statements or anything that makes the product look like medicine.
6. Reuse rights for the video, and rules for AI voiceovers and virtual models.

Clear clauses help both sides. The brand lowers its risk of fines, and the KOC knows exactly what they can say.

Where AI wins: the first five minutes. Calling a web lead within 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you 100 times more likely to reach them (MIT and InsideSales.com Lead Response Management Study).

The No. 1 belief about AI and engineering teams is that it shrinks them. (90% of US tech leaders say they're keeping or growing theirs.)

That's from Karat's 2026-2027 AI Workforce Transformation Report (The Harris Poll for Karat, 157 tech leaders in the US and China, Oct 8). Among US tech leaders:
90% use AI to produce more while keeping or growing their engineering teams. Just 10% are holding output steady with fewer engineers.
82% report more product and feature volume from AI.
67% also report longer time to bring new features to market, and 44% report more coding errors.
Globally, 75% say a strong engineer is worth at least 3x their compensation.

So AI raises output, and the review, testing and release work grows with it. That work needs senior people.

As a CTO, that's how I'd set up 2027: count the roles by what they'll review and own, then decide which are full-time, contract or augmented, and when each seat has to be filled.

I recently asked AI to help me put together an illustrated story for my son’s class. In one scene, a little boy makes an elephant shadow with his hand. The elephant looked lovely. Unfortunately, one of the boy’s fingers had a trunk of its own. 🐘

That one was easy to spot. Flashy, the main character, was trickier. Each picture looked fine on its own. It was only when I read the pages in order that I realised how different she looked from one to the next. I’d been asking, “Does Flashy look right on this page?” A better test was to turn the page. Would a four-year-old recognise her, or would I have to stop the story to explain, “Yes, that’s still Flashy”? 😄

I made a similar call when I led an HR platform team. We needed to check that payroll could calculate a new starter’s first payslip. I also wanted to know whether the start date HR entered was the one payroll actually used. That changed where we started the test.

Take someone who signs their contract on 1 June, starts work on 16 June and earns €3,000 a month. I’d pick those two dates deliberately. HR enters both in the hiring system, an engineer checks which one reaches payroll as the start date, and payroll runs the June payslip. Using calendar days, we’d expect €1,500 in gross base pay. If the system sends the date they signed, we’d see €3,000. If both dates were the same, the test would pass either way.

We could have typed 16 June straight into payroll, got €1,500 and ticked the test off. Starting in hiring let us check what would happen when HR put a real person through that process.

As for Flashy, she now looks like herself all the way home. I have a feeling my son’s class will let me know if I’ve missed anything else. 😊

AI is not firing your team yet. It may already be firing your vendor.

Anthropic interviewed 58 of its enterprise customers. They saw very few domestic layoffs driven by AI. But most companies said they are hiring less because of it, and nine described cutting contracted developers, customer service, legal and back-office work, much of it already offshored.

The common thread: modular tasks, handed off as self-contained pieces, were the easiest to replace. One executive said it plainly: "We've since fired them because now we can get better quality things faster and cheaper."

For anyone in Latin America selling services to US or European companies, or building a partner channel on top of those services, this is the warning. If your contract is a list of tasks, a model is now competing for it.

The partners that keep the account will be the ones who own a whole workflow and answer for the result.

Buyer's-Eye Check #1: Robert Half. Score: 6/10.

I looked at their US home page the way a hiring manager would on a first visit.

1. Five-second test: 2/4.
The headline says "Anything's Possible When You Have the Talent." Swap the logo and it fits any firm on earth. The first block speaks to job seekers. The person who pays, the employer, comes second.

2. What Google and ChatGPT can read: 3/3.
This part is solid. The page title and description say exactly what they do. Nothing blocks AI crawlers. Easy to quote.

3. Path to a conversation: 1/3.
No phone number, no email, no form on the home page. A busy manager has to click into a menu of about 30 services to find a person.

The three fixes I'd make first:
1. Make the headline the job: "Hire finance, tech and legal talent in days, contract or full time."
2. Split the first screen: one button for employers, one for job seekers, employers first.
3. Put a phone number and a short "tell us the role" form on the home page.

A giant can get away with a vague headline. A 20-person firm can't.

What would yours score? Comment "check" and I'll run the same three boxes on your site.

Your next customer might not speak English. And for the first time, that's not a problem you need a big budget to solve.

A few years ago, "going multilingual" meant hiring translators, managing localisation agencies and paying per word for every page, email and product description. For most small businesses it simply wasn't worth it, so they stayed local by default.

AI translation has quietly changed the maths. Modern models don't translate word by word; they read the full meaning of a sentence and rewrite it naturally in another language. The jump in quality is striking, and it compounds across everything you publish.

Where it actually shows up for a business:
- A website that greets each visitor in their own language.
- A support chat that answers in dozens of languages at once.
- Product pages, emails and even live calls translated in real time.

The result is simple: a shop in London can sell to the whole world without a localisation department. The barrier to reaching global customers just got dramatically smaller.

A word of caution: it isn't magic. For contracts, safety information and anything high-stakes, keep a human in the loop to review. AI gets you most of the way at near-zero cost; a person closes the last stretch where it matters.

"People lose their jobs and businesses shut down because of people like you."

I hear this from time to time. It's not meant as a compliment.

A task comes up at work: an analytics pipeline, automated content review, an internal service. I explain how we solved it with AI: faster, far cheaper, without adding headcount. Then it turns out that for the person across the table, this was someone's job, someone's contract, or an entire SaaS business.

Cue the monologue: "We spent years on architecture and a team. Then people like you vibe-code something over a weekend and call it our product. It won't scale. Where's the security? Where's the SLA? It's a toy."

Let's be honest: they're right. If that's you, you're right. But only half right.

Where they're right: the market is flooded with weekend hacks built by people who never read the code they generated. Those fall over under real load, leak data, and are easier to throw away than to fix. And if you run regulated infrastructure with bank-grade resilience, a three-line prompt won't replace you. Not yet.

Where they're wrong: they take the worst of amateur vibe coding and stretch it over all AI-assisted development.

Serious AI engineering is still a full SDLC. Only the production tool has changed:
• clear architecture and separation of layers
• a system of prompts, skills, and validation rules
• MCP connections to real databases and tools
• deterministic tests and automated checks

Built this way, my projects ship 5–10x faster at a fraction of the cost. Few companies can still afford millions in subscriptions and bloated teams just to test a hypothesis or close an internal task.

The market has already billed those who sold routine at the price of complexity:
• Chegg has lost more than 90% of its market value since ChatGPT launched.
• Stack Overflow was already losing questions. AI turned the slide into a cliff, and the company cut 28% of its staff in 2023.

The limits are just as visible. Klarna said its AI assistant did the work of 700 support agents. About a year later it was hiring humans again because quality had slipped, while the bot kept two-thirds of the chats. Routine went to AI. Judgment didn't.

Models living on borrowed time:
• content mills selling basic copy and SEO text
• scripted first-line support
• template landing pages and cookie-cutter MVPs
• routine translation, transcription, and data labeling

Businesses don't close because someone learned to use AI. They close because they spent too long selling inefficiency as "deep expertise."

This isn't about three vibe coders in boxers with $20 subscriptions saving the world. It's about the fact that nobody needs pagers, the Yellow Pages, or mail-order catalogs anymore.

An AI org chart lays out your AI like staff, and mine has 11 roles.
⠀
1 job per role, its own instructions, and a clear line for who it hands the work to when the job isn't its own.
⠀
Most owners I talk to use one AI chat for everything. The same window writes the email, prices the job, answers the tax question and reviews the contract, and it starts from zero every time. That's like hiring one person and asking them to be your bookkeeper, your salesperson and your accountant on the same afternoon.
⠀
An org chart splits that up. Each role gets one job, the reference material for that job and the background on your business, and it knows where its job ends.
⠀
These are 4 of mine, in my AI operating system (AIOS):
⠀
1. My bookkeeper knows my actual chart of accounts, so it tells me which account each transaction goes to and which tax code goes on it.
2. My tax coach answers what I can deduct, and it has to point to the government source for every answer it gives me.
3. Anything about filing goes past both of them to my accountant, who's a real person, because that's where the line is.
4. My council has three roles: one argues against my idea, one argues for it, and the third weighs both and gives me a verdict.
⠀
And honestly, the council is the one I use the most before a big decision, because it's the only one built to tell me I'm wrong.
⠀
The point isn't how many roles you have. It's that every job has an owner, and you know who to ask.
⠀
---
⠀
P.S. If you drew your AI side as an org chart today, how many boxes would be on it?
⠀

Last Thursday, we hosted Rethinking In-House Legal with the FT Live to discuss how legal teams are keeping up with growing demands.

It was a pleasure to bring everyone together, and we hope everyone who joined us enjoyed the discussion as much as we did and came away with useful ideas for their own teams.

Two takeaways we keep coming back to:
- Give the business one place to ask legal anything, and let AI triage it. If people can't get a quick answer from legal, they'll ask a chatbot instead and you'll never see it - leading to shadow legal.

- AI in the business is adding to legal’s workload. As sales and marketing use it to move faster, more contracts and questions land on legal’s desk. Hiring alone won’t close that gap. There’s a clear case for legal AI in helping the team keep up, without making job cuts the justification.

Huge thanks to our GC Lucy Tyrrell, to Suzi Ring for chairing, and to Adele Falconer, Georgia Byrne, Andie Garford-Tull (杜颖嘉) and Vicki Bradin for such an open discussion.

A difficult UK economy can give businesses a reason to change their leadership, not just freeze recruitment.

There are reports of renewed momentum in UK executive hiring despite economic challenges. That does not prove the economy is causing an increase, but it raises an important distinction: recruiting more leaders and recruiting a different kind of leader are not the same thing.

For CEO, MD and COO appointments, we have noticed a "human" centred shift in the brief recently to combine strong commercial acumen with a genuinely human-centred approach.

That means someone who understands margins, cash flow and growth, but also spends time with employees, listens to clients and customers, and acts on what they hear.

Those are not competing priorities. A customer conversation can expose a service problem before it becomes a lost contract. Customers, Clients and Employees are looking to Executive Leadership to inspire, engage, trust and lead. Listening to and hearing what employees and customers/clients are saying can reveal that 1% of difference that delivers longer term commercial value and success.

With the speed and advancement of technology and tech innovation/AI, we are starting to realise what skills/behaviours are important and it always comes back to human connection with tech enabled efficiency. 

From a Search perspective, the assessment needs to test both sides. Alongside the standard sales/commercial and revenue we need to think deeper and get "under the bonnet" of the people we meet.

At Disrupt we refer to "People Architecture" and see this as a key component of any Search or recruitment process.  

Emotional intelligence and the ability to adapt to your environment is now a non-negotiable to long term survival. Without this how can we win the hearts and minds of the people to put in the hard work so we can all thrive? 

So how are Boards, Co-founders and Executive leadership assessing this?

Are you going beyond the standard questions at interview stage or just recycling the process created in the 1980's?

Truly understanding the people that you are trusting to lead your business should not be underestimated; ask candidates for evidence of how they handled difficult decisions, retained trust, transformed engagement, and test how they received feedback and altered their course for success. 

The strongest appointment should not require a choice between commercial discipline or human engagement. The brief should demand evidence of both.
